newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO, Israel contact resumes in settlement shadow.
newsitem.headline: PLO, Israel contact resumes in settlement shadow.

text.p: Israeli-Palestinian contacts, severed by the PLO over the Jewish state's policies, resumed as a by-product of a dramatic visit by Jordan's King Hussein to Israel but their future still looked shakey.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, at a news conference with the king in Jerusalem on Sunday, said they both spoke by telephone to Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Arafat, enraged at Israel's plans to build a new Jewish settlement close to Arab East Jerusalem, had twice refused to receive Netanyahu envoys in the last 10 days.
Netanyahu said he hoped the conversation would put Israel's dialogue with the Palestinians on a new footing.
But he also vowed that Israel would start construction of the new Jewish settlement that has angered King Hussein as well as the Palestinians.
Asked if bulldozers would move onto the hilltop site during the next day or two, Netanyahu said: "I said that they would start this week. They will start this week."

Israeli cabinet secretary Danny Naveh later confirmed to Reuters that final status peace talks between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO), set to resume on Monday, would not take place as planned.
Netanyahu spokesman Shai Bazak, asked what contacts, if any, would take place between the two sides on Monday, said: "At the moment it's not clear."

Neither Netanyahu nor the king elaborated on their talks with Arafat. But Netanyahu's communications director David Bar-Illan, asked if there was an effort to get Netanyahu and Arafat together, told Reuters: "You can say that."
Israel Radio later quoted a Palestinian source saying there were contacts for a meeting in the next two days between Netanyahu and Arafat, but this could not be confirmed.

In a gesture to the Palestinians, Netanyahu said Israel would allow Arafat to use the Gaza Strip airport of Dahanya and an agreement on that might be signed on Monday. Full operation of the airport is a still unresolved issue.

King Hussein visited Israel to console families of seven schoolgirls shot dead by one of his soldiers at the border last week and to defuse tensions with Netanyahu over a harsh letter he wrote to the prime minister.
Jordanian officials said the gunman acted alone and the king told the parents of victim Sivan Fatihi, 13: "Your loss is my loss, my personal loss."

The king's letter echoed Palestinian officials who had warned of possible bloodshed if Israel went ahead with unilateral plans to begin work on the 6,500 houses for Jews at the site known as Jabal Abu Ghneim in Arabic and Har Homa to Israelis.

Netanyahu says the settlement reasserts Israel's right to all of Jerusalem and insists that Israeli-PLO peace deals do not bar the construction. Palestinians claim East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967, as the capital of a future state.
